etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English sure, seur, sur, from Middle French sur or Old French seür, from Latin sēcūrus (“secure”, literally “carefree”), from sē- (“apart”) + cūra (“care”) (compare Old English orsorg (“carefree”), from or- (“without”) + sorg (“care”)). See cure. Doublet of secure and the now obsolete or dialectal sicker (“certain, safe”).

Displaced native Middle English wis, iwis (“certain, sure”) (from Old English ġewis, ġewiss (“certain, sure”)), as well as Middle English siker (“sure, secure”) (from Old English sicor (“secure, sure”)) with which it was cognate.

This etymology is incomplete. You can help Wiktionary by elaborating on the origins of this term. When and how did the letter"s" come to be pronounced as "sh"? The OED entry points to a source that may have information on this: E. J. Dobson Eng. Pronunc. 1500–1700 (ed. 2, 1968) II. §185 (iii.) and $388. Perhaps early irregular yod-coalescence?

definitions.definition: Physically secure and certain, non-failing, reliable.

quote.citation: 1932, Aldous Huxley, Brave New World‎[1], London: Chatto & Windus:
quote.text: 'In the end,' said Mustapha Mond, 'the Controllers realized that force was no good. The slower but infinitely surer methods of ectogenesis, Neo-Pavlovian conditioning and hypnopædia…'

definitions.definition: Certain in one's knowledge or belief.

quote.citation: 1827, Thomas De Quincey, On Murder Considered as one of the Fine Arts:
quote.text: The very excess of the extravagance, in fact, by suggesting to the reader continually the mere aeriality of the entire speculation, furnishes the surest means of disenchanting him from the horror which might else gather upon his feelings.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter IV, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC, page 58:
quote.text: The Celebrity, by arts unknown, induced Mrs. Judge Short and two other ladies to call at Mohair on a certain afternoon when Mr. Cooke was trying a trotter on the track. The three returned wondering and charmed with Mrs. Cooke; they were sure she had had no hand in the furnishing of that atrocious house.

quote.citation: 2008 November 21, Graham Linehan, The IT Crowd, Season 3, Episode 1:
quote.text: Roy: I'm 95% sure it was him.Jen: You... you said you were 99% sure.Roy: I'm 97% sure it was him.

definitions.definition: (followed by a to infinitive) Certain to act or be a specified way.

quote.citation: c. 1590–1591 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Two Gentlemen of Verona”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i], page 36, column 1:
quote.text: Feare not: the Forreſt is not three leagues off, / If we recouer that, we are ſure enough.

quote.citation: c. 1513-1518 (probably date written, published after 1535) Thomas More, History of King Richard III
quote.text: The king was sure to Dame Elizabeth Lucy, and her husband before God.
I presum'd  […]  [that] you had been sure, as fast as faith could bind you, man and wife.
These high and gusty relishes of life, sure,Have no allayings of mortality in them.

quote.citation: c. 1587–1588, [Christopher Marlowe], Tamburlaine the Great.  […]  The First Part […], 2nd edition, part 1, London:  […]  [R. Robinson for] Richard Iones, […], published 1592, →OCLC; reprinted as Tamburlaine the Great (A Scolar Press Facsimile), Menston, Yorkshire, London: Scolar Press, 1973, →ISBN, Act II, scene iii:
quote.text: Theſe are the wings ſhall make it flie as ſwift,As dooth the lightening: or the breath of heauen,And kill as ſure as it ſwiftly flies.

definitions.definition: Yes, expressing noncommittal agreement or consent.
You're welcome; polite response to being thanked.
